Technical Design — Real-Time Face Recognition Attendance System

Below is a complete, developer-ready technical design for your project. It covers architecture, components, data flows, algorithms, APIs, data models, deployment options, security/privacy, testing, and a phased implementation plan — plus concise code snippets you can drop into a prototype.

1. High-level architecture (components)

Camera / Capture Layer (Edge)


Webcam / IP camera(s) (RTSP) / CCTV feed.


Capture module pulls frame

s at configurable FPS.


Processing Layer (Edge or Server)


Face detection (OpenCV Haar/Cascade or DNN/caffe/onnx model / MediaPipe).


Face alignment & preprocessing (crop, resize, histogram equalization).


Face encoding (face_recognition / dlib embeddings).


Face matching / recognition (compare against stored encodings).


Duplicate prevention & debounce logic (avoid marking multiple times in a timeframe).


Persistence & Storage


Attendance store (CSV for MVP; relational DB like PostgreSQ

L or SQLite for production).


User profiles with face encodings (files, DB BLOBs, or separate encoded JSON).


Audit logs and unknown-face snapshots.


API & Backend


Lightweight REST API (Flask/FastAPI) to: register users, upload images, query attendance, export reports, admin actions.


Optional WebSocket for real-time UI updates (dashboard).


UI / Dashboard


Admin dashboard for enrollment, reports, manual overrides, and alerts (React or plain HTML for MVP).


Notifications / Integration

Email/SMS push (Twilio/SMTP) for parent recognition/dismissal alerts.


Integrations with School MIS / LMS via exported CSV or API adapters.


Monitoring & Ops


Logging (file + rotated logs), metrics (Prometheus / simple counters), error reporting.


2. Data flow (sequence)

Camera captures frame → Processing Layer receives frame.


Detect faces → For each face: align & encode.


Compare face encoding with known encodings database (nearest neighbor / threshold).


If match found and not alread

y marked in recent window → mark attendance (persist record).


If unknown face above a threshold → store unknown snapshot + alert admin.


Send events to Dashboard / Notifications / External systems.


3. Detailed components & algorithms

3.1 Face detection

Options:


Haar Cascade (OpenCV) — fast, less robust.


DNN face detector (jk) — deploy.prototxt + res10_300x300_ssd_iter_140000.caffemodel — more robust.


MediaPipe Faces — great speed and pose robustness.


Recommendation: Use OpenCV DNN

or MediaPipe for production; Haar only for very low-resource prototypes.


3.2 Face embedding / recognition

Use face_recognition (dlib under the hood) to compute 128D embeddings.


Matching strategy:


Precompute encodings for all enrolled users.


Use cosine similarity or Euclidean distance. face_recognition provides compare_faces and face_distance.


Choose threshold (typical: 0.45–0.6 for Euclidean depending on dataset). Tune with validation images.


3.3 Duplicate prevention / Debounce

Ke

ep an in-memory dict: {user_id: last_seen_timestamp}.


If now - last_seen_timestamp < debounce_window (e.g., 60s or class length), do not re-mark.


For persistent state across restarts, keep recent marks in DB.


3.4 Handling unknown faces

If no match found and face confidence > threshold:


Save snapshot + timestamp + camera_id.


Optionally present to admin for manual enrollment or discard.


Rate-limit unknown alerts to prevent flooding.


3.5 Enrollment flow

Admin uploads 3–10 images per

user (varied lighting/angles).


System computes encodings and stores them with the profile.


Optionally capture a short video to extract frames and auto-generate encodings.

7. Hardware & dep

loyment

Edge (on-prem) vs Cloud

On-prem/Edge: run recognition on local PC or Raspberry Pi (better for privacy, lower bandwidth). Use faster CPU + optionally a GPU (NVIDIA Jetson / GPU) for higher throughput.


Cloud: stream frames to cloud inference (costly, privacy concerns). Use when central monitoring and multi-site aggregation needed.


Recommended specs (classroom / small school)

Small (single classroom): modern laptop with 8GB RAM, i5 CPU, standard webcam.


Multi-class/scale: dedicated

server with GPU (NVIDIA T4 / RTX 2060+), 32GB RAM, SSD.


Edge low-cost: Raspberry Pi 4 + Coral TPU for model acceleration (requires porting to TF-Lite).


Camera placement & settings

Frontal camera at 1–2m height, angle slightly downward.


Ensure even lighting; avoid strong backlight.


Configure resolution trade-off: 720p often sufficient; higher resolution increases CPU.


8. Security, privacy & compliance

Data minimization & consent

Collect minimal data; require parental/staff consent.

Provide opt-out flow (manual sign-in alternative).


Storage & encryption

Encrypt encodings and stored images at rest (e.g., AES-256).


Use TLS for API and any networked camera streams.


Access control & audit

Role-based admin access.


Audit logs for enrollment / access / data exports.


Legal & policy

Check local regulations: FERPA, GDPR, state laws on biometric data (e.g., Illinois BIPA).


Provide retention policy: e.g., delete raw frames after X days; keep attendance data per school

policy.


Spoofing / Liveness

Add simple liveness checks: blink detection, head pose change, or challenge-response using short prompts.


For sensitive deployments, consider hardware with anti-spoofing SDKs (IR sensors, depth cameras).


9. Performance & scaling

Metrics & targets

Latency per detection: target <200ms for detection + recognition combined (edge optimized).


Throughput: determine frames-per-second processing, e.g., 5–10 FPS is typical for real-time attendance.


Accuracy: target

>95% in controlled conditions; design to degrade gracefully.


Scaling strategies

Batch query encodings using efficient search:


KD-Tree, Annoy, Faiss for approximate nearest neighbor when known set > 10k.


Shard per classroom / camera: each camera has its own small known set to speed matching (if students per camera limited by class rosters).


10. Testing & validation

Unit & Integration tests

Unit tests for encoding generation, matching thresholds, CSV writing, API endpoints.


Integrati

on: simulated camera stream with varied images; measure recall/precision.


Accuracy testing

Create a labeled dataset (same lighting variance as production).


Measure FAR / FRR at thresholds. Choose threshold to balance false positives vs negatives.


End-to-end pilot

Run a 2–4 week pilot in 1–3 classes. Log:


Time saved per roll call.


False acceptance/rejection rates.


User feedback (teachers, parents, students).


Iterate on thresholds, camera placement, enrollment instructions.


11. F

ailure modes & mitigations

Low light / occlusion → fallback to manual sign-in or alternative ID scanning.


Network outage (cloud) → local caching and sync later.


High false positives → tighten threshold, add liveness tests, increase enrollment images diversity.


Privacy objections → offer opt-out and secure data deletion.


12. Roadmap / Implementation phases

Phase 0 — Preparation (1–2 weeks)

Gather camera hardware & sample images; finalize consent policy.


Phase 1 — MVP (4–8 weeks)

Imp

lement real-time detection & recognition; CSV output; basic UI to enroll users.


Pilot in one class.


Phase 2 — School roll-out (2–4 months)

Add REST API, dashboard, parent notification, duplicate suppression, unknown snapshot review.


Integrate with school MIS (CSV export/ETL).


Phase 3 — Scale & polish (3–6 months)

Add analytics dashboards, cloud sync, optimization with ANN search, anti-spoofing, and SLA.


Hardening: monitoring, logging, encryption, multi-site deployment.


13. Monitori

ng & maintenance

Daily health checks: camera ping, process alive, disk usage.


Automated backups of DB and export to secure storage.


Maintenance tasks: retraining/updating face models, updating enrollment images.

4) How to run

Option A — Run locally (recommended for development)

Create a virtualenv, activate it.


pip install -r requirements.txt (this may take time because of dlib).


Run the API:

 uvicorn app.main:app --reload

Enroll a user:

 curl -X

POST "http://127.0.0.1:8000/enroll" -F "name=alice" -F "file=@/path/to/alice.jpg"

Run the webcam client (in another terminal):

 python webcam_client.py

The client will send periodic frames to POST /recognize. When person matches and isn't debounced, attendance will be appended to app/storage/attendance.csv.


View API docs at: http://127.0.0.1:8000/docs


Option B — Docker (API only; webcam client must run outside container)

Build:

 docker build -t attendance-mvp .

Run:

 docker run --rm

-p 8000:8000 -v $(pwd)/app/storage:/app/app/storage attendance-mvp

Note: containerization of webcam is complex; simplest approach: run webcam client locally and point it to http://<docker-host>:8000/recognize.

6) Limitations & practical notes

face_recognition / dlib build: building dlib inside Docker can be slow and sometimes fails on resource-constrained systems. If you see build errors, two options:


Run the app locally where you already have dlib working (easier).


Use a base image that already has dlib installed (search for dlib prebuilt images) or use a wheel for your platform.


Webcam in Docker: accessing host webcams from a container requires extra flags

(e.g., --device=/dev/video0) and is platform-dependent. For the MVP, run the webcam client locally.


Performance: this MVP uses naive matching (linear scan). For larger rosters (>500 users) use Faiss/Annoy for ANN search.


Privacy: ensure consent & data protection. This MVP stores encodings locally in app/storage/encodings.json (not encrypted).


Liveness: this MVP has no anti-spoofing. Add liveness checks for production.


Debounce: simple time-window. Adjust per class timing.
